← Event seating chart optimizer

How to make a wedding seating chart

A seating chart looks like a drawing job and is really a puzzle: dozens of small wishes, a hard limit on seats per table, and a few people who must be at a particular table. Done by hand it takes an evening of moving names around, and every fix for one wish can break another.

Open the free seating chart optimizer

The method

1. List everyone, and tag the families. Put the same party name after each member's name so they are treated as a group that wants to sit together.

2. Write the wishes as pairs. Who should sit together, who really should, who to keep apart if you can, and who must never share a table.

3. Pin the fixed seats. The couple's parents, the officiant, the head table: pin each to a table number and the search leaves them there.

4. Score and search. Every pair at the same table adds or removes points, and the plan with the best total within capacity wins. Look at the unmet wishes, decide which you can live with, and run it again for another arrangement.

A worked example

Twenty-four invented guests, three tables of eight, and eight wishes: two families (the Okafors, four people, and the Brandts, three), four pairs who should sit together, and two feuds: Uncle Ray must be kept apart from Aunt Linda and never share a table with Victor Lang. Maya Okafor and Priest Anselm are pinned to table 1, Liam Brandt to table 2.

SeatingWishes metFamilies splitScore
In the order typed4 of 8154
Optimized8 of 8081

Seating in list order puts Uncle Ray with Aunt Linda, parts Priya Nair from Tom Whitfield, Cousin Ben from Cousin Jess and Elena Petrova from Hannah Cole, and splits the Brandts across two tables. The search meets all eight wishes, keeps both families whole and keeps the pins, with eight at every table.

What the plan leaves out

It assigns tables, not seats within a table, and it knows only the wishes you typed: not who gets on, dietary needs, wheelchair access or the shape of the room. It is a starting point for you and your planner, not a promise that every guest will be happy.

Questions

How do I seat people who should not sit together?

Mark the pair with a single exclamation mark to keep them apart if possible, or two to forbid sharing a table. The optimizer treats a never-together pair as outweighing almost any friendship, so it separates them even when that splits a group of friends. If a never-together pair is still seated together, the plan lists it.

Does list order matter?

Only as a baseline. The guide's example seats the same 24 guests in the order typed, which meets 4 of 8 wishes and splits one family across two tables, and the optimizer meets all 8 with every family intact.

How many guests should sit at each table?

Round tables commonly seat 8 to 10, and a banquet table can run longer. The tool takes seats per table as an input and by default fills tables evenly, so 24 guests across 3 tables give 8 each.

how-to-seat-divorced-parents-at-a-weddin.text:
← Event seating chart optimizer

How to seat divorced parents at a wedding

Divorced parents are the classic seating problem: two people who may not want to share a table, each with a new partner, each with relatives who take a side. The way through is to decide it once, as written rules, rather than re-deciding it every time you move a name.

Open the free seating chart optimizer

The method

1. Give each side its own table. Pin each parent to a table number (Nina Castillo @ 1) so the head tables are settled before the search runs.

2. Forbid the one pairing that must not happen. Marta Reyes !! Karen Moss means never the same table. Use ! for pairs who are merely better apart.

3. Keep each parent with their partner. Put the same party name after both names, or add a + wish, and they travel together.

4. Add the friendships, then read what is left. The plan lists any wish it could not meet so you can decide which you can live with.

A worked example

Twenty-four invented guests, three tables of eight, and ten wishes. Nina and Paul Castillo (one side) are pinned to table 1, Marta and Dev Reyes to table 2, and Karen and Alan Moss to table 3. Marta Reyes must never share a table with Karen or Alan Moss, Dev Reyes is better apart from Karen, and Beth Lowe is better apart from Dana Price. Karen Moss wants to sit with Beth Lowe, Dev Reyes with Pat Quill, and four more pairs of friends and relatives want to be together.

SeatingWishes metParties splitScore
In the order typed7 of 10024
Optimized10 of 10036

List order happens to keep the former spouses apart only because the pins hold them; it still seats Beth Lowe with Dana Price and parts Karen Moss from Beth Lowe and Dev Reyes from Pat Quill. The search meets all ten wishes with eight at every table.

What the plan leaves out

It assigns tables, not seats within a table, and it knows only the wishes you typed: not who has stopped speaking to whom, custody or travel arrangements, dietary needs, wheelchair access or the shape of the room. Talk to the people involved. It is a starting point for you and your planner, not a promise that every guest will be happy.

Questions

Where should divorced parents sit at a wedding?

Give each side its own table near the front, and keep the two tables apart. Pin each parent to a table number and mark the former spouses with two exclamation marks so the optimizer will never put them at the same table, even to satisfy a friendship.

Should a divorced parent's new partner sit with them?

Usually yes: a new partner is a guest of that parent, so list them together as one party and the optimizer keeps them at the same table. Seat the new partner away from the other parent only if the people involved ask for it; the tool follows the wishes you type, not a rule about who belongs where.

What if two people are fine but not close?

Use a single exclamation mark. It tells the optimizer to keep the pair apart if it can, but lets it seat them together when the table maths needs it, and the plan lists any such pair so you can decide.

EVENT SEATING CHART OPTIMIZER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Who sits where? Let the search sort your seating chart.

Paste your guest list, add who should sit together, who to keep apart and who is pinned to a table. The optimizer assigns every guest to a table with the most wishes met, within capacity, and shows you any it could not.

A planning aid for you and your family or planner. New to this? Read how to make a wedding seating chart, with a worked example. Divorced parents or a feud? See how to seat divorced parents.

1. Guests and wishes

Have the list in a spreadsheet? Paste the rows here, or . Columns named Name (or First and Last), Household or Party, Side or Group, Meal and RSVP are recognised; declined RSVPs are left out. Read in your browser, never uploaded.

A + B sit together · A ++ B really together · A ! B keep apart · A !! B never at one table · A @ 3 pin to table 3

2. Tables

Add your guests and wishes, then click Seat my guests.

Your guests, wishes and settings are remembered on this device only (browser local storage), so you can come back as RSVPs arrive.

Seating plan

Wishes it could not meet

    Groups by table

      Meals by table

        3. Someone dropped out or RSVP'd late?

        Edit the guest and wish boxes above, paste the CSV you downloaded last time, and re-seat. Guests who are still coming stay at their table unless moving them is worth it, so you do not have to redo place cards or tell forty people they moved.

        How it works

        Scoring: every pair of guests that shares a table adds to a score. Members of the same party add 6, a + adds 3, a ++ adds 12, a ! takes away 6 and a !! takes away 200. The plan with the highest total wins, so a feud is separated even if it splits a friendship.

        Search: simulated annealing moves and swaps guests between tables, accepting some worse moves early so it does not get stuck, restarted six times; a hill-climbing pass then applies any move or swap that still helps. Table capacity and pinned tables are never broken. The same list gives the same plan until you ask for another arrangement. On small events the answer is checked against trying every possible arrangement.

        Not modelled: seat order within a table, couples at a head table sitting in a row, wheelchair access or room layout, grouping guests by dietary need (a fourth column only tallies meals for the caterer), which tables are near the stage or the door, children's tables as a rule, and how much one person dislikes another beyond the four strengths. Unverified against a real event: tested against exhaustive search on hundreds of small random lists and on a 200-guest list.

        Common questions

        How do I make a wedding seating chart?

        List every guest, mark who comes together as a party, add the pairs who must or should sit together and the pairs who should be kept apart, then fix anyone who has to be at a particular table, such as the couple or a parent. The optimizer then assigns everyone to tables so the most wishes are met within each table's capacity. You can rerun it for a different arrangement and edit by hand afterwards.

        How does the seating optimizer decide who sits where?

        Every pair of guests gets a score: parties and wanted pairs add points, avoided pairs subtract points, and a never-together pair subtracts a very large number. It searches for the assignment with the highest total, using simulated annealing followed by a hill-climbing polish, within table capacity and pinned tables. On small events its answer is checked against trying every possible arrangement.

        What do + ++ ! !! and @ mean?

        Write one rule per line. A + B means they should sit together. A ++ B means they really should. A ! B means keep them apart if you can. A !! B means never at the same table. A @ 3 pins a guest to table 3.

        Can I keep families together?

        Yes. Put the same party name after a bar on each family member's line, such as Maya Okafor | Okafor family, and the optimizer treats every pair in that party as a wish to sit together. If a party is larger than a table it says so and shows which tables it was split across.

        What if there are more guests than seats?

        The tool tells you how many seats you are short and does not produce a plan. Raise the seats per table or the number of tables. Leave the number of tables blank and it uses the fewest that fit.

        Does it spread guests evenly across tables?

        By default yes: each table is filled to about the same level so you do not end up with one packed table and one nearly empty. Untick the option to let tables fill up to their full capacity instead.

        What if a guest drops out after I have sent the seating plan?

        Edit the guest list, paste the CSV you downloaded last time into the re-seat box and click Re-seat. Guests who are still coming stay at their table unless moving them is worth it, so only a few people move and the rest of your place cards stay valid.

        Is the guest list uploaded or stored?

        It is never uploaded. Everything runs in your browser, nothing is sent to a server and there are no accounts. So you can come back as RSVPs arrive, your guest list, wishes and settings are remembered on this device only (browser local storage); click Forget saved data to remove them, or save a setup file to move to another device. Download the plan as a CSV to keep the result.

        Is the plan guaranteed to be the best possible?

        No. It is a search, so on a large event there may be a slightly better arrangement, and it only knows the wishes you typed. It is a starting point to review with your family or planner, not a substitute for judgement about people. Check the table-by-table list before printing place cards.
